data.body:
OPERATOR CONSTRAINT ADDED (2026-09-03) — this changes the sizing model for S1/S2 and may expose a gap in the approved design.

Operator: '~10 plan reviews run in parallel frequently, which causes disk pressure that CANNOT be pruned until the reviews finish. That is in addition to disk pressure from code reviews and auto-deploy.'

## The code confirms the mechanism exactly

`src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py` documents its own design: it relies on POSIX **delete-on-last-close** plus touch-on-read mtime recency, and deliberately takes **no per-reader lease** — a PID+heartbeat lease was spiked and REJECTED as unsound (N readers per entry, PID reuse, crash-stale leases), following Gitaly/Sourcegraph/Bazel/ccache. It also skips any entry inside a short grace window.

The consequence is the operator's point, stated in the code's own terms: the janitor may UNLINK an in-flight snapshot, but under delete-on-last-close the blocks are not returned until the last reader closes. **So during peak concurrency, reclamation is structurally ineffective — the bytes are live, not garbage.**

## Why this matters for the approved design

Option A caps each accumulator via native GC at a high-water mark. **A high-water-mark GC assumes evictable data exists.** Under ~10 concurrent reviews it largely does not: the space is held by live readers and by grace-window entries. A cap set below peak concurrent hold cannot be honoured — the GC will run, find nothing evictable, and the volume fills anyway. That is the same shape as the failure this epic exists to fix: four rounds of prune-based mitigation that could not reach the bytes that mattered (~6.5 GB of orphaned overlay2 invisible to prune, per bug 3276's measurement).

So the sizing rule has to be: **cap >= peak concurrent hold**, not cap = steady-state target. And S1's dedicated gate-scratch volume must be sized for PEAK, not average.

## Two mitigating and two aggravating factors

MITIGATING: the snapshot store is CONTENT-ADDRESSED, so N concurrent reviews against the same base share one snapshot rather than holding N copies. And snapshots stream to disk with a 512 MiB cap per `workflow/snapshot.py`.
AGGRAVATING: the review-bot CLONE is per-review and not shared — `voter.py:381` opens `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='reviewbot-')` per review, so clones scale linearly with concurrency. And the operator notes code reviews and auto-deploy add pressure on the same volume concurrently.

## The design gap this exposes — needs an operator decision

The approved design (Option A caps + Option C separate volume) contains **no admission control**. If peak concurrent demand exceeds the provisioned volume, no cap value can help — the choices are a volume sized for peak, or a limit on how many reviews may hold scratch at once. Sizing for peak alone is unbounded in principle: the ceiling becomes 'however many reviews someone launches'.

Recorded as an open question rather than decided, since the design is operator-approved and this is a genuine addition to it, not a re-litigation.

## Also settles the bug 9ea3 OOM arithmetic

A COMPLETE plan-review measured today at ~739 MB resident delta. Ten in parallel is ~7.4 GB on an 8 GiB box already carrying gerrit 0.88 GB + mcp 1.08 GB + review-bot 0.17 GB + opcert 0.04 GB. That is a definitive OOM explanation and closes the gap I flagged earlier, where a single ~500 MB gate against ~2.3 GiB headroom did not account for the kill.
